papers.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
papers.abstract: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

papers.title: scCTM: Continuous Thought Machine Reconstruction of Glioma Cell Fate Dynamics Attractor Landscapes and Algorithmic Perturbation Signatures
papers.abstract: Cell fate plasticity dynamics in glioma ecosystems is usually inferred from static single-cell snapshots, leaving a gap between manifold geometry, predictive modelling, and mechanistic intervention ranking. We developed scCTM, a complexity theory and machine learning framework that combines the Sakana AI Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) with autoencoding, a continuous actor-critic policy over synchronization-derived latent states for predicting single-cell fate dynamics. We also incorporated integrated-gradient and decoder-weight explainability, network science, empirical Waddington-like landscape (attractor) reconstruction, and post-hoc Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis. The complexity framework was evaluated in two malignant cell secondary analyses: GSE210567 stem-like versus differentiated H3K27M cells (18,490 cells) and longitudinal H3K27M initial versus recurrent disease trajectory (20,000 cells) from Sussman et al. (2026) as a ML binary classification problem. CTM-AE achieved AUROC values of $0.99$ in both datasets. CTM-RL preserved classification almost exactly but did not improve reconstruction. Out-of-fold CTM-RL latent states produced potential basins across PCA, UMAP, and PHATE embeddings. BDM edge perturbation analysis further identified recurrent high-impact network interactions, including epigenetic/chromatin-associated signatures involving ARID1B and developmental or neuronal-state genes such as AUTS2, CTNND2, DPP6, NRXN1, and CADM2. These in silico findings support CTM synchronization as an interpretable latent-state representation and predictive forecasting of cell fate dynamics, as well as BDM perturbation signatures as a complementary in silico intervention ranking layer for systems medicine.
